template.why: §5.5's context rule, and deliberately identical to law.trial-preparation so that a user who never separates jury material from the rest of trial prep gets one coherent branch rather than two half-filled ones (§5.9's warning about levels that produce one child).

collides_with.signal: jury material is a subset of trial preparation in most practices and a separate workstream in a few. Whether it deserves its own branch is a §5.3 vertical-pass decision the user makes, not one this catalogue makes.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Juror questionnaires and selection research contain private information about named individuals who are not parties. No handling class is set here.
entries.open_question: This domain does not exist in large parts of the world, and where it exists it varies enormously — civil juries in some systems and not others, extensive selection procedures in some and none in others, and juror information that is restricted in some jurisdictions and open in others. Should a domain that is inapplicable to most corpora ship in the library at all, or activate only when a `jurisdiction` fact indicates a jury system? §3.11's rule — a schema activates 'when the evidence indicates that a domain is plausible' — is a per-file test, not a per-corpus one, and this is the clearest case where a per-corpus gate might be needed instead.

entries.name: Hearing transcripts and the record of proceedings
entries.one_line: The verbatim record of what happened in front of a court or tribunal, and the indexes into it.

schema.example: the identifier in the transcript caption
schema.why: Transcripts are captioned like pleadings and join to the proceeding by the same key.

schema.example: the court or tribunal sitting
schema.why: Distinguishes a hearing transcript from an out-of-court examination transcript, which is otherwise formally identical.

schema.example: the sitting date
schema.why: Stated on the cover as a labeled slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies. Load-bearing here because multi-day hearings produce one file per day and the days must stay ordered.

schema.example: which day of a multi-day hearing
schema.why: Stated on the cover. Without it, day 2 and day 12 sort as though they were versions of one document.

schema.example: rough | uncertified | certified | corrected
schema.why: Stated on the cover or in a certificate. Different statuses of the same day are NOT a version family in the ordinary sense — a rough and a certified transcript are both authoritative for different purposes — and merging them loses that.

deterministic: a page-and-line numbered transcript whose cover page names a court AND a case identifier AND a sitting date
a transcriber's certificate block co-occurring with a case identifier
a transcript index or key-passage index citing page and line references, carrying a case identifier
needs_llm: a rough transcript delivered as plain text with no cover page
an audio recording of a hearing where only a transcript would identify it — §2.9 permits speech-to-text “only under an explicit privacy and compute policy”
distinguishing a hearing transcript from an examination transcript when the cover is missing
never_alone: page-and-line numbering
the word 'transcript'
a court name appearing in body text — judgments, articles and textbooks name courts constantly
a date

grouping_reasons: all days of one hearing
a transcript with the index and notes citing it
successive statuses of one day's record

template.why: §5.5's context rule; matches law.trial-preparation so a hearing's bundle and its transcript live under the same hearing node. Day is ordering within the type, not a level — §5.9 warns against levels that create many tiny folders.

collides_with.signal: formally near-identical. The court name and the judge are what separate them.
05 lists 'transcript' among its work types. A transcript a party holds is 05's; this entry needs a matter and a practice-side signal.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Openness of a hearing record varies by jurisdiction and by proceeding, and some hearings are closed entirely. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Settlement negotiation and settlement instruments
entries.one_line: The offers, the exchanges and the agreement that ends a dispute without a decision.

schema.why: Settlement material often deliberately omits the case identifier; the practice's own reference is usually all that remains.

schema.example: the parties to the agreement
schema.why: The signing parties can differ from the litigating parties — a parent, an insurer or a guarantor may sign — which is why §3.8's roles rule requires this to be its own field rather than reusing `party`.

schema.example: offer | counter-offer | agreed terms | executed agreement
schema.why: The stage is on the face of the document and is the whole meaning of the file: an offer and an executed agreement have opposite consequences and identical wording.

schema.example: the execution date
schema.why: A dated execution block is a labeled slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies.

schema.example: the proceeding being settled, where stated
schema.why: Present on consent orders and discontinuance documents; frequently absent from the private agreement itself.

deterministic: a document containing a release or discharge clause AND a payment or consideration clause AND a matter reference
an offer letter carrying a settlement-privilege or negotiation legend together with a matter reference or case identifier
a consent order or discontinuance document carrying a case identifier
needs_llm: an email exchange in which an offer is made and accepted with no formal document
distinguishing a settlement agreement from an ordinary commercial contract, where the release clause is the only structural difference
identifying which of several exchanged drafts is the executed version when none is signed
never_alone: a release clause — commercial contracts, employment agreements and licence terms all carry them
a negotiation or privilege legend on a letter: the legend is text on the page and does not establish any legal status (see law.document-review's open_question)
the word 'settlement' — it also means a payment settlement, a housing settlement and a geographic settlement
a payment amount

grouping_reasons: one negotiation from first offer to executed agreement
the agreement with the consent order that implemented it
drafts of one agreement as a version family (§2.9's “duplicate and version-family signals”)

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Deliberately shallower than the litigation domains: a settlement is a single episode of a matter and §5.8's uneven-depth allowance applies — “The product should not force every branch to use the full template”.

collides_with.signal: a settlement agreement is a contract, and a party's own signed copy is that party's record. It belongs here when it carries a matter reference or resolves an identified proceeding; otherwise it DEFERS.
a mediated settlement is produced inside an ADR process. The agreement is this domain; the mediation process record is that one.
05 lists 'settlement agreement' among its work types. The negotiation apparatus — offers, counter-offers, drafts under a matter reference — is this entry; a party's executed settlement is 05's.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Settlement terms are frequently subject to confidentiality obligations owed to a third party, which is a reason to protect the file and not a reason for this catalogue to assign a class. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Mediation and arbitration
entries.one_line: A dispute resolved outside the courts — the appointment, the submissions, the process record and the award or outcome.

schema.example: the case number an institution assigns
schema.why: Institutional references have their own formats, distinct from court identifiers, and an ad hoc process may have none at all — so this is a separate field from `case_identifier` rather than a reuse of it.

schema.example: the institution administering the process, or ad hoc
schema.why: The forum determines the rules, the vocabulary and the document set. It is normally named on the face of every document in the reference.

schema.example: mediation | arbitration | expert determination | adjudication
schema.why: These processes have different structures and different outcomes, and merging them makes the file unreadable. Availability and naming differ by jurisdiction and by contract, so values are corpus-derived.

schema.example: the arbitrator, tribunal or mediator
schema.why: Named in the appointment document and the award header — labeled slots. §3.8's roles rule keeps this distinct from `deciding_judge` and from `authored_by`.

schema.example: a party to the reference
schema.why: Read from the header block. Party designations differ from litigation designations in most rules sets, which is why the vocabulary is not shared with law.pleadings.

deterministic: a document header naming an arbitral or mediation institution AND a reference identifier AND two or more parties
an appointment or terms-of-reference document naming a neutral and the parties who appointed them
an award document whose structure pairs a reasons section with a numbered dispositive section, carrying an institutional reference
needs_llm: an ad hoc process with no institution and no reference, identifiable only from the correspondence
distinguishing a mediation position paper from a litigation submission, which it closely resembles
recognising an arbitration clause dispute inside ordinary contract correspondence
never_alone: the word 'arbitration' or 'mediation' — arbitration clauses appear in ordinary commercial contracts and terms of service that no dispute has ever touched
an institution's name appearing in a contract clause
the word 'award' — it also means a prize, a grant and a contract award
the word 'neutral'

grouping_reasons: one reference from notice to award
all documents before one tribunal
an award with the enforcement or challenge material that followed

template.why: §5.5's context rule. 'Reference“ rather than ”proceeding' because the identifier and forum differ from the court family, and a matter can run a court proceeding and an arbitration at the same time — which the tree must keep apart.

collides_with.signal: arbitral submissions are pleading-shaped. The institutional reference and the absence of a court name are the distinguishing signals.
see that entry — the mediated agreement versus the mediation process record.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Most arbitration is private and many rules sets impose confidentiality on the parties, which makes the file sensitive as a matter of fact. No handling class is set here.
entries.open_question: Arbitral confidentiality is a real obligation owed to a counterparty rather than a privacy interest of the corpus owner, and §8.4's handling classes run from 'Public or low sensitivity' to “Highly sensitive or credential-bearing” and are all framed around personal sensitivity. Is an obligation owed to someone else an axis P7's vocabulary needs, or does it collapse into the existing classes? This is a P7 vocabulary question raised here, not answered here.

entries.name: Legal research and authorities
entries.one_line: The record of finding out what the law is — memoranda, research notes, and the authorities collected to support them.

schema.example: the question the memorandum answers
schema.why: Stated as prose under an issue or question heading. §3.5 places this squarely with the LLM; §3.6 requires the cited span to exist.
Matter-specific research belongs to its matter. Its ABSENCE is the signal that the file belongs to the know-how library instead — see law.knowhow-precedents.

schema.example: the legal system researched
schema.why: The most important field in this domain and rarely stated in a slot. Research answering a question under one system is actively misleading if filed as though it answered it under another.

schema.example: the area of law addressed
schema.why: Prose interpretation. The value vocabulary is corpus-derived; §3.12: “The system may create new values when it sees a new course, project, company, university, or event, but it should not invent new fields automatically.”

schema.example: a cited case, statute or instrument
schema.why: Held for search and explanation, never for placement. A file must not be placed by what it cites: §3.8's principle that a folder must not become 'a collection point' applies to cited authorities as much as to authors.

deterministic: a memorandum whose heading block pairs an issue or question line with a conclusion or advice line, carrying a matter reference
a dense citation-bearing document co-occurring with a matter reference AND practice-side context such as a fee-earner block or an 'our ref' line
a saved authority — a judgment, statute extract or database print — filed alongside a memorandum carrying the same matter reference
needs_llm: an untitled research note with no matter reference
distinguishing research prepared for a matter from reading kept out of interest
reading which jurisdiction the research addresses when it is implicit in the authorities cited
never_alone: case or statute citations — this is the single largest false-positive source in the whole supercategory. Law review articles, textbooks, student essays, journalism, policy papers, compliance training and terms of service all cite law heavily and none of them is legal-practice work product
the word 'memorandum' — it names internal business notes of every kind
a legal database export or watermark
the words 'held', 'pursuant to', 'notwithstanding'

grouping_reasons: a memorandum with the authorities collected for it
all research on one matter
research on one question across matters

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Topic sits below matter because research is done FOR a matter; the know-how domain inverts this deliberately, which is the clearest structural difference between the two.

collides_with.signal: the same memorandum becomes know-how when it is de-identified and kept for reuse. A matter reference is what keeps it here.
a law student's research essay is citation-dense and issue-structured. §3.5's course rule wins where a course code and academic context are present, and this domain must abstain rather than compete.
collides_with.design_cite: §3.5 “becomes a course fact only when the engine finds a course-code pattern together with academic context”

collides_with.signal: legal scholarship is research, not practice. Absence of a matter reference plus presence of academic apparatus should route it away from this slice.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. A research memorandum states a client's legal position and its weaknesses. No handling class is set here.
entries.open_question: Citation identifier patterns are already catalogued for the research slice (`planning/deferred-catalogues/06-citation-identifier-patterns`), which covers DOI, ISBN, URL and author-year forms. Legal citation is a separate and jurisdiction-specific system — case citations, statute references and law-report abbreviations differ by country and have no cross-system standard. Should legal citation be added to catalogue 06, kept as a separate per-jurisdiction catalogue, or refused entirely on the ground that a citation is `possible` here and never placement-bearing?

entries.name: Opinions and formal advice
entries.one_line: A formal, addressed statement of legal position that a client or a third party is entitled to rely on.

schema.example: the addressee entitled to rely
schema.why: §3.8's field. An opinion is addressed, and the addressee is the point — reliance is what distinguishes it from a research memorandum.

schema.example: the practice giving the opinion
schema.why: §3.8's paired field. An opinion received FROM another practice is a different artefact from one the practice gave, and merging them would be a serious error.

schema.example: the question opined on
schema.why: Prose. §3.6 requires the cited span before it becomes a fact.

schema.example: the date the opinion bears
schema.why: A dated signature block is a labeled slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies. Load-bearing because an opinion speaks as at its date.

schema.example: the law opined on
schema.why: Formal opinions state the governing law explicitly, usually in a scope or assumptions section, which makes this one of the few places the jurisdiction is a readable slot rather than an inference.

deterministic: an addressed letter containing an assumptions or qualifications section AND an opinion or conclusion section, on practice letterhead
a document with a stated reliance or addressee-limitation clause together with a practice signature block
a counsel's opinion carrying an instructing-practice reference and a set of instructions attached
needs_llm: advice given in an ordinary letter or email with no formal structure
distinguishing a formal opinion from a research memorandum where neither is labelled
recognising a draft opinion that was never given
never_alone: the word 'opinion' — it names reviews, editorials, survey responses and audit opinions
practice letterhead — practices send marketing and administrative letters on it
the phrase 'in our view'
an assumptions section

grouping_reasons: an opinion with the instructions that produced it
successive opinions on one question
all opinions given to one client

template.why: §5.5's context rule; kept shallow because an opinion is a small, discrete deliverable and §5.8 allows a branch to stay flat where the extra levels would each hold one file.

collides_with.signal: a memorandum informs the practice; an opinion is given to a recipient who may rely on it. The addressee and the reliance language are the signals.
a transaction opinion is a closing deliverable and belongs to the deal's closing set as well as here.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. An opinion states a considered legal position and its qualifications. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Precedent bank and know-how
entries.one_line: Reusable material kept for the next matter rather than for the one it came from — model documents, clauses, checklists and standing notes.

schema.example: the kind of reusable document
schema.why: Know-how is organised by what a document IS, since by definition it belongs to no matter. Read from the title or a know-how header.

schema.example: the area the precedent serves
schema.why: Prose interpretation. This is the primary retrieval dimension for the whole domain, which is why it sits above document type in the template.

schema.example: the system the precedent is drafted for
schema.why: A precedent used under the wrong system is worse than no precedent. Rarely stated; usually inferable only from the drafting.

schema.example: the version or last-reviewed marker
schema.why: Know-how goes stale, and a superseded precedent that looks current is the characteristic failure of a precedent bank. §2.9's “duplicate and version-family signals” apply directly.

schema.example: the matter the precedent was derived from, where recorded
schema.why: Kept at `possible` on purpose. A precedent derived from a real matter should NOT be pulled back into that matter's folder by this field, and a value here must never drive placement — see this entry's open_question.

deterministic: a document containing drafting placeholders — bracketed or bracketed-and-capitalised insertion markers — in a document type that is otherwise a finished instrument
a drafting note or guidance-note structure interleaved with clause text
a know-how header block naming a topic and a review or version marker, with no matter reference
needs_llm: a real executed document kept as a model with the names left in
distinguishing a firm precedent from a published model form or an industry standard document
reading the topic and the jurisdiction from the drafting alone
never_alone: placeholder brackets — templates of every kind use them, including invoices and letters
the words 'template', 'precedent' or 'model' — 'precedent' also means a prior decision, which is a different thing entirely, and 'template' is universal
absence of a matter reference: most files in a corpus have none
a checklist

grouping_reasons: a precedent with its drafting notes
all know-how on one topic
successive versions of one precedent as a version family

template.why: The one domain in this slice with NO client and NO matter level, which is the whole point of it. §5.5's rule still governs — topic is the context that makes a clause bank interpretable — but the spine is subject rather than engagement.

collides_with.signal: a precedent derived from a real matter carries that matter's fingerprints. The absence of a live matter reference plus the presence of placeholders should keep it here; a stray retained reference must not drag it back.
precedent pleadings are pleading-shaped with dead captions. See law.pleadings.
05's 'NDA' and standard-form work types can be indistinguishable from a precedent. Placeholders and the absence of a counterparty are what keep a file here; a party's own template of its NDA is 05's.

entries.sensitivity_why: A properly de-identified precedent carries no client or personal content. This is the only entry in the slice not marked potentially_sensitive, and the marking is conditional on the de-identification actually having happened — an imperfectly redacted precedent is a matter document and should be recognised as one.
entries.open_question: A precedent is often a de-identified copy of a real matter document, so a content-similarity signal will pull the two together and §2.9's duplicate/version-family logic may treat them as versions of one file. Does the product need an explicit rule that a know-how copy is never grouped with its source matter, and if so is that a grouping stop rule (§4.9 already lists stop rules) or a placement rule? Getting this wrong leaks a client document into a library that is shared across the practice.

entries.name: Transactional deal file
entries.one_line: The file of one transaction — the parties, the structure, the documents that make it happen and the record of getting there.

schema.example: the name or code the transaction is run under
schema.why: Transactions are almost always given a working name that appears on every document, and it is frequently a code name that reveals nothing — which makes it a reliable key precisely because it is arbitrary.
Joins the deal to the engagement. A deal may run across several matters and several practices.

schema.example: the kind of transaction
schema.why: Rarely labelled; read from the principal document. The vocabulary is partly jurisdiction-bound and values are corpus-derived.

schema.example: a principal to the transaction
schema.why: Read from an execution or parties block. §3.8's roles rule is acute here — a party may be buyer, seller, lender and guarantor across one deal's documents.

schema.example: which side of the transaction a party sits on
schema.why: The side is what makes the file navigable and is almost never stated as a label; it is read from the role a party takes in the operative documents.

schema.example: draft | agreed form | execution version | executed
schema.why: The single most consequential field in transactional work: a draft and an execution version are textually near-identical and legally opposite. Usually stated in a header or footer marker.

deterministic: a document with a parties block AND an execution block, carrying a deal name or matter reference in a header or footer
a document status marker in a header or footer — a draft, agreed-form or execution-version legend — together with a deal name
a document list or checklist naming the deal and enumerating the instruments required to complete it
needs_llm: reading the transaction type and each party's side from the operative documents
identifying which of a series of near-identical drafts was the one executed, when no marker distinguishes them
recognising that a code-named document set is one transaction
never_alone: a contract — the corpus is full of contracts and almost none belong to a legal practice's deal file
an execution block or signature page
a code name — project code names are used for products, campaigns and reorganisations too
the words 'agreement', 'party', 'consideration'

grouping_reasons: one transaction across all its instruments
one instrument across its drafts as a version family
documents produced at one stage of one deal

template.why: §5.5's context rule with 'deal' where the litigation domains have 'proceeding'. §5.5's second rule is what rules out a date-first tree — 'putting year first scatters related work across calendar folders' — and a deal's drafts span months.

collides_with.signal: the deal file is the ADVISER's file; the executed contract in a party's own records is that party's. A file with drafts, checklists and a document list is this domain; a lone executed PDF with no surrounding apparatus DEFERS.
negotiation work product is a phase of a deal. Where a practice runs contract negotiation as a standing function rather than per-deal, that domain stands alone.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. A live deal file is commercially confidential and often price-sensitive. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Due diligence and disclosure
entries.one_line: The examination of what is being bought or lent against, and the counterparty's formal disclosure of what is wrong with it.

schema.example: the transaction the diligence serves
schema.why: Diligence output is meaningless outside its transaction and is normally headed with the deal name.

schema.example: the entity or asset examined
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule: the target is not the client and is often not a party to the practice's engagement at all. Merging it into `client` would be the characteristic error here.

schema.example: the area examined
schema.why: Diligence is run in parallel workstreams that produce separate reports and separate data-room folders; the workstream is normally the document's own heading.

schema.example: the index reference of a reviewed document
schema.why: Data-room indexes are numbered structures and the reference is a labeled slot, so `direct` per §3.5. It is the only durable link between a report finding and the document behind it.

schema.example: the warranty a disclosure is made against
schema.why: A disclosure schedule is meaningless except against the numbered warranty it qualifies; the pairing is the document's structure.

deterministic: a report whose section structure follows named diligence workstreams AND that cites indexed document references
a data-room index — a numbered hierarchical document list — carrying a deal or target name
a disclosure schedule whose rows pair a numbered warranty reference with disclosure text
a requests list paired with a responses column, headed with a target name
needs_llm: a diligence summary written as prose with no workstream headings
distinguishing a diligence report from an audit, a valuation or a technical assessment of the same target
recognising a data-room export whose index was not included
never_alone: a numbered hierarchical file index — every large document set has one
the words 'due diligence' — the phrase is used loosely in procurement, hiring and vendor management
a company name
a findings or issues list
the word 'disclosure' — it also names financial and regulatory disclosure, which are different domains

grouping_reasons: one diligence exercise across its workstreams
a report with the data-room documents it cites
a disclosure letter with its schedules and the warranties they answer

template.why: §5.5's context rule; a finding is unreadable outside its workstream and its deal. Matches law.transactional-deal's first two levels deliberately so diligence sits inside the deal rather than beside it.

collides_with.signal: both produce entity lists. See law.conflicts-check.
a data room and a production are both large indexed document sets delivered between parties. The production has a load file and party direction; the data room has a hierarchical index and a target.
diligence is a workstream of a deal; it is a separate domain because its schema — target, workstream, index reference — is genuinely different from the deal's.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. A data room routinely contains a target's employment records, contracts and account information — material §8.4 names directly, held about people and entities who are not the corpus owner's clients. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Signing, closing and completion
entries.one_line: The act of completing a transaction and the compiled record of what was signed and delivered.

schema.example: the transaction completed
schema.why: The binder exists only as the record of one deal; without the deal name it is an unattributable stack of signed documents.

schema.example: the date completion occurred
schema.why: Stated on the binder cover and the completion certificate as a labeled slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies. Unusually load-bearing here: the completion date is the identity of the event.

schema.example: the tab or item number in the index
schema.why: A binder index is a numbered structure, so the reference is a labeled slot per §3.5. It is how every later query into the binder is phrased.

schema.example: delivered | outstanding | waived
schema.why: A completion checklist states this per item, and it is the difference between a closed deal and one with open obligations.

schema.example: execution version | executed
schema.why: Carried over from law.transactional-deal deliberately, so an execution version and the executed original are never merged into a version family.

deterministic: a binder or bible index pairing tab numbers with document titles, headed with a deal name and a completion date
a completion or closing checklist whose rows pair required deliverables with a status column, headed with a deal name
a compiled PDF whose bookmarks reproduce a numbered document list and whose members are executed instruments
needs_llm: a stack of signed PDFs delivered without an index
distinguishing an execution version circulated for signature from the signed original returned
never_alone: a compiled PDF with bookmarks
signature pages
the word 'closing' — it names accounting periods, sales cycles and shop hours
a numbered document index

grouping_reasons: one completion event and everything delivered at it
a binder with the deal file it completes
outstanding post-completion items across a deal

template.why: §5.5's context rule, kept shallow because the binder's own index already supplies the internal ordering and reproducing it as folders would create exactly the “large number of tiny folders” §5.9 warns about.

collides_with.signal: the binder is the deal file's terminal artefact, and every document in it also exists as a deal draft. §6.9's shared-material policy governs which copy is the primary home.
collides_with.design_cite: §6.9 “a shared branch, a primary-home convention, a reference or alias convention, or mandatory review”

collides_with.signal: the client's own copy of the binder is that client's record. The practice's compiled binder with its checklist apparatus is this domain; a client's lone executed set DEFERS.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. A binder contains executed originals, signatures and often account details — §8.4 names 'account statements' among the corpus's sensitive material. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Contract drafting and negotiation work product
entries.one_line: The legal function's record of getting a contract agreed — playbooks, marked-up drafts, issue lists and approvals.

schema.example: the organisation on the other side of the draft
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule; the counterparty is the spine practitioners navigate contract work by, and it is not the client and not the author.

schema.example: the kind of agreement being negotiated
schema.why: Read from the operative provisions rather than a label. Values are corpus-derived per §3.12.

schema.example: which exchange a draft belongs to
schema.why: Negotiation produces long chains of near-identical files. Round is what makes them a sequence rather than an undifferentiated version family, and it is normally in the filename or a footer.

schema.example: which side marked up this draft
schema.why: The single most useful fact in a negotiation folder and the easiest to lose. §3.8's roles rule again — it is a role, not authorship metadata.

schema.example: an open point tracked across the negotiation
schema.why: Issue lists are prose tables. §3.6 requires the cited span before an issue becomes a fact.

schema.example: the internal approval a deviation carries
schema.why: Playbook-driven negotiation records deviations and who approved them; stated in a labeled slot on the approval record.

deterministic: a contract document containing tracked-change or comment metadata (§2.3's DOCX structure) together with a counterparty name in a footer or filename convention
an issues or open-points list pairing clause references with positions taken by each side
a playbook document pairing standard positions with fallback positions per clause
needs_llm: a clean redraft with the tracked changes accepted, where the round is only recoverable from the covering email
distinguishing a negotiation draft from a template and from an executed contract
reading which side proposed a change when the markup is anonymised
never_alone: tracked changes — every collaborative document has them

a contract document: this is the loudest false positive in the slice, because every corpus contains employment contracts, leases, terms of service and supplier agreements that no legal function ever negotiated
the word 'draft'
a clause-numbered structure

grouping_reasons: one contract across its negotiation rounds as a version family (§2.9's “duplicate and version-family signals”)
all contracts with one counterparty
a playbook with the negotiations it governed

template.why: §5.5's context rule with counterparty as the spine, because in-house contract work is not organised by matter and often has no matter at all. Round is ordering within the contract, not a level: §5.9 warns against 'a large number of tiny folders'.

collides_with.signal: slice 05 owns a contract as a party's own record — the signed lease, the supplier agreement. This domain owns the NEGOTIATION APPARATUS around it: playbooks, marked-up rounds, issue lists, deviation approvals. A file with only an executed contract and no apparatus DEFERS to slice 05.
a deal's drafts are negotiation work product too. Where a code-named transaction exists, the deal domain is the better home; this domain covers standing contract work with no deal.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Negotiation work product records the positions a party was prepared to concede. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Corporate secretarial and entity records
entries.one_line: The constitutional and decision-making record of a legal entity — constitution, registers, minutes and resolutions.

schema.example: the company or other body the record belongs to
schema.why: The organising spine of the whole domain. A group corpus holds dozens of entities and a minute filed against the wrong one is worse than a lost minute.

schema.example: the registration number in the entity's home registry
schema.why: The only unambiguous entity key, since names repeat and change. Formats are registry-specific and jurisdiction-bound, so the field is neutral and no pattern is authored here.

schema.example: the kind of constitutional record
schema.why: Read from the title block. §3.11 already uses `record type` as a Finance field name and it is reused rather than renamed.

schema.example: the date of the meeting or resolution
schema.why: Minutes and resolutions are dated in a labeled header slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies.

schema.example: the board, a committee, or the members
schema.why: Different bodies have different powers and their records must not merge. Stated in the header of every minute.

deterministic: a minute document whose header pairs an entity name with a meeting date AND a decision body, followed by resolution or noting text
a written resolution containing an entity name, a resolution number or heading, and a signature or consent block
a statutory register — a table of officers, members or charges — headed with an entity name and registration number
needs_llm: a draft minute circulated before approval
distinguishing board minutes from ordinary management meeting minutes, which look identical
recognising which entity in a group a resolution belongs to when only a trading name is used
never_alone: meeting minutes — every organisation produces them and almost none are board minutes
the words 'resolution', 'board' or 'register' — all are ordinary business words, and 'resolution' also means screen resolution and dispute resolution
a company name
a signature block

grouping_reasons: one entity's constitutional record
one meeting with its agenda, papers and minutes
a group's entities as a related set

template.why: §5.5's context rule with entity as the spine and NO client level, because corporate secretarial work is organised by the entity whose record it is even when a practice keeps it for a client. §5.5's rule against time-first applies with full force — a constitutional record is a continuous history, not a series of years.

collides_with.signal: a company's own corporate records are that company's business records. This domain applies where the material is maintained as a legal-function or company-secretarial record; a business owner's own copy of their incorporation certificate DEFERS to slice 05.
registry filings are both entity records and regulatory submissions. The filing confirmation belongs here; the substantive regulatory application belongs there.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Registers carry officers' and members' personal details and addresses. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Regulatory filings and submissions
entries.one_line: What is submitted to a regulator or public authority, and what comes back.

schema.example: the authority the submission goes to
schema.why: The domain's spine. Regulators are jurisdiction-specific bodies and the gazetteer of them is not authored here — see law.matter-file's open_question.

schema.example: the reference the authority assigns
schema.why: Formats are per-regulator, so the pattern is not hard-coded; the reference becomes a fact through the corroboration in recognition.deterministic.

schema.example: the entity on whose behalf the submission is made
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule: the submitting entity is frequently the client, sometimes a group member, and never the practice — three distinct roles that must not merge.

schema.example: the regime or form the submission is made under
schema.why: Read from the form header. Regimes and their forms are jurisdiction-bound and values are corpus-derived.

schema.example: the date of lodgement or the receipt date
schema.why: A receipt or acknowledgement carries a labeled timestamp. §3.10's narrow parsing applies and no deadline is computed.

deterministic: a completed authority form — labeled fields plus a form identifier in a header or footer — together with a named authority
an acknowledgement or receipt from a named authority carrying a submission reference
a covering letter addressed to a named authority citing a regime and a reference
needs_llm: a substantive submission written as a narrative document with no form structure
distinguishing a regulatory submission from a grant application, a tender or a licence renewal notice
recognising a foreign authority by name alone
never_alone: a completed form — the corpus is full of forms of every kind
an authority's name appearing in body text: compliance training, news articles and terms of service name regulators constantly
the word 'regulatory' or 'compliance'
a reference number

grouping_reasons: one submission with its supporting material and the authority's response
all submissions to one regulator for one entity
a submission with the internal approvals behind it

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Regulator before submission because a regime's vocabulary only makes sense once the authority is known. §5.8's uneven depth applies — a single-submission matter should collapse the last two levels.

collides_with.signal: registry filings sit in both. See that entry.
a programme document describes what the organisation does; a submission is what it told an authority. Very different consequences, similar vocabulary.

05's entry is the same act from the submitting entity's side and carries `filing_entity`, `filing_period` and `submission_reference`. This entry claims the advising practice's file — the supporting submission, the drafts, the authority correspondence run under a matter. Slice 05 owns the party's own file; this slice owns the practitioner's. The mover is a practice-side signal — a matter reference, a fee-earner or counsel signature block, practice letterhead, an engagement letter. Absent one, this slice ABSTAINS and 05 wins. This is 05's own specialisation rule applied across the seam: 'the more specific domain wins where its own fields populate'.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Submissions frequently contain financial and personal information about the submitting entity and named individuals. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Compliance programme materials
entries.one_line: The standing apparatus by which an organisation tries to stay compliant — policies, training, monitoring and attestations.

schema.example: the risk area the material addresses
schema.why: Read from the substance; policy titles are frequently generic. §3.6 requires the cited span before it becomes a fact.

schema.example: the organisation the programme belongs to
schema.why: Distinguishes an organisation's own programme from a counterparty's policy received during diligence — the same document type with the opposite meaning.

schema.example: the version or effective-date marker
schema.why: A superseded policy that looks current is this domain's characteristic failure. §2.9's “duplicate and version-family signals” apply.

schema.example: policy | procedure | training | monitoring record | attestation
schema.why: These have very different audiences and retention profiles and are routinely mixed in one folder.

schema.example: the stated effective or review date
schema.why: Stated in a labeled control block on most policies. §3.10's narrow parsing applies.

deterministic: a document control block — pairing a version, an owner and an effective or review date — inside a document whose title names a policy or procedure
an attestation or acknowledgement record pairing named individuals with a policy version and a date
a monitoring or testing record pairing control descriptions with testing outcomes, headed with an owning entity
needs_llm: training material with no control block, where only the content shows it is compliance training rather than general onboarding
distinguishing an organisation's own policy from a policy received from a counterparty or downloaded as a market example
never_alone: the word 'compliance' — it appears in engineering, accessibility, tax and product contexts constantly
a policy document: HR, IT and security policies dominate most corpora and none of them is legal-function work product
a training deck: this is the hazard this entry exists to name — compliance training is deliberately written in legal vocabulary and will match any rule keyed on legal words alone
a legal citation inside a policy

grouping_reasons: one programme area across its policy, training and monitoring
successive versions of one policy
an attestation cycle as a bounded set

template.why: §5.5's context rule with no client or matter level, because a compliance programme is a standing function rather than an engagement. Where an external practice advises ON a programme, that advice belongs to law.opinions or law.matter-file instead.

collides_with.signal: compliance training a person COMPLETED is that person's career record; compliance training an organisation MAINTAINS is this domain. A completion certificate naming an individual should route to slice 02.
a programme failure produces an investigation. The programme document is standing; the investigation is an episode.
a counterparty's policies collected in diligence are diligence material, not the corpus owner's programme. `owning_entity` is what separates them.

05's entry is entity-level compliance EVIDENCE and audit — auditor, framework, audit period. This entry is the standing programme apparatus: policy, training, monitoring, attestation. They meet where an audit tests a programme, and 05's row already says an audit a regulator required produces documents that are both.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Attestation and monitoring records name individuals and record their conduct. Policies themselves are frequently not sensitive at all, which is why the marking sits at the domain level and the actual handling decision stays with P7 (§8.4).

entries.name: Investigations
entries.one_line: A bounded enquiry into what happened — the plan, the evidence collected, the interviews and the findings.

schema.example: the practice's or organisation's own reference for the enquiry
schema.why: Investigations are frequently run without a case identifier and with deliberately uninformative names; the reference is often the only reliable key.

schema.example: who instructed the investigation
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule, and consequential: an investigation commissioned by a board, by a regulator or by a counterparty are three different things with three different postures.

schema.example: the question the enquiry was set to answer
schema.why: Stated in a terms-of-reference document as prose. §3.6 requires the cited span.

schema.example: a strand of the enquiry
schema.why: Investigations run parallel strands — document collection, interviews, forensic analysis — that produce separate outputs.

schema.example: the role a person had in the events, not their name
schema.why: Deliberately a ROLE field rather than a person field. §3.8 requires roles as distinct facets, and an investigation file is the place where naming individuals as a folder dimension would do the most harm — §3.8: “A folder should not become a collection point for everything produced by the same person or organization.”

deterministic: a terms-of-reference document pairing a commissioning party with a stated scope, carrying a matter or investigation reference
an interview memorandum whose header pairs an interviewee designation with a date and an attendee list, under a common investigation reference
a findings or report document whose structure pairs allegations or issues with conclusions, under an investigation reference
needs_llm: material collected during an investigation that carries no investigation marking at all
distinguishing an investigation interview memorandum from an HR grievance record or a journalist's interview notes
reading the scope from a covering email when no terms of reference exist
never_alone: the word 'investigation' — it names product, security, medical and journalistic work
interview notes
a findings or issues list
an allegation-shaped sentence

grouping_reasons: one investigation across its workstreams
interview material from one enquiry
a findings report with the evidence it cites

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Workstream before document type because an interview memorandum and a forensic report belong to different strands and mixing them destroys the enquiry's shape.

collides_with.signal: an investigation is usually opened as a matter. It has its own entry because its schema — commissioning party, scope, workstream — is genuinely different, not because it sits outside the matter.
investigations run document review. Same work product, different purpose — §3.9's distinction: “Topic answers what a file is about, while purpose answers what the file was for.”
collides_with.design_cite: §3.9 “Topic answers what a file is about, while purpose answers what the file was for.”

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. An investigation file records allegations about named individuals, frequently before anything is established, and §4.9's protection principle applies: “Rare but sensitive files such as passports, visas, and legal documents may be surfaced as protected records even when they do not meet a normal group-size threshold.” No handling class is set here.
entries.open_question: Investigation files are the strongest case in this slice for a protection posture stronger than the general legal safety domain — they record unproven allegations about identified people, and §8.4's classes are framed around the corpus owner's own sensitivity rather than third parties'. Whether P7's vocabulary needs a class for material that is sensitive about SOMEONE ELSE is a P7 question raised here and not answered here. It applies equally to law.family-law, law.criminal-defence and law.immigration-casework.

entries.name: Intellectual property prosecution
entries.one_line: Obtaining and maintaining registered rights — applications to an IP office, the office's objections and the responses.

schema.example: the office the application is before
schema.why: The domain's spine. One invention or mark is prosecuted before many offices simultaneously and the files must not merge.

schema.example: the number the office assigns
schema.why: Formats are per-office and the same right carries a different number in every office, which is why this is a validated field with office corroboration and never a bare pattern match.

schema.example: the practice's own reference tying related filings together
schema.why: The only thing that links one right's filings across offices. Usually the practice's own docket reference rather than any official number.

schema.example: patent | trade mark | design | other registered right
schema.why: Different rights have different procedures and different documents; the type is on the face of every office communication.

schema.example: the entity in whose name the right is sought
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule: applicant, inventor and owner are three roles that frequently name different people and are routinely conflated.

schema.example: the stage the document belongs to
schema.why: Prosecution is a long sequence of exchanges and the stage is stated on each office communication. Stage names are office-specific and values are corpus-derived.

deterministic: an office communication whose header pairs a named IP office with an application number AND an applicant name
a specification document containing both a claims section and an abstract, together with an application or docket reference
a docket or renewals report pairing family references with office deadlines
needs_llm: a draft specification before filing, with no application number
distinguishing prosecution material from IP litigation and from IP licensing, which share vocabulary and parties
recognising an office communication in an unfamiliar language
never_alone: the words 'patent', 'trade mark' or 'copyright' — they appear in product documentation, marketing, terms of service and academic writing
a claims-and-abstract structure: a scientific paper has an abstract too
an application-number-shaped string
a priority date

grouping_reasons: one right's family across offices
one office's file from filing to grant
an office action with the response it drew

template.why: §5.5's context rule with the family above the office, so one invention's national filings stay together rather than being scattered across office folders — the same reasoning §5.5 gives for keeping a course above its work types.

collides_with.signal: an invention disclosure and a draft specification are research artifacts by content. The office, the application number and the claims structure are the practice-side evidence; without them slice 03 should win.

an IP office is an authority and a filing is a submission. This domain exists separately because its schema — family, right type, prosecution stage — is genuinely different and its files are long-running.

near-total overlap by document type — 05 lists application, office action, response, grant, renewal, assignment. 05 owns them as the rights holder's record; this entry owns the prosecuting practice's docket, with the family reference across offices as its distinguishing field. Where there is no practice-side signal, 05 wins.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Unpublished applications are commercially confidential and their premature disclosure has consequences. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Immigration casework
entries.one_line: An application or claim made on a person's behalf to an immigration authority, and the evidence assembled for it.

schema.example: the person the application is for
schema.why: The spine of the file. §3.8's roles rule keeps the applicant distinct from a sponsor and from the client, who are frequently three different people or an employer.

schema.example: the authority the application is made to
schema.why: Determines the route vocabulary, the form set and the identifier format — none of which is authored here because all of it is jurisdiction-specific.

schema.example: the route or category applied under
schema.why: Stated on the form. Route names and their meanings differ completely between countries and change often, so values are corpus-derived and this catalogue equates none of them.

schema.example: the reference the authority assigns
schema.why: Formats are authority-specific; corroboration is required as in every other identifier field in this slice.

schema.example: the employer, institution or family member supporting the application
schema.why: §3.8's roles requirement. The sponsor is frequently the paying client while the applicant is the subject — a distinction that must survive into the fact layer.

deterministic: a completed authority application form — form identifier plus labeled applicant fields — together with a named immigration authority
an authority decision or acknowledgement letter carrying a case reference and an applicant name
a supporting-evidence bundle index listing identity, status and relationship documents, under a common case reference
needs_llm: a personal statement or narrative account prepared for an application
distinguishing a legal practice's casework file from an individual's own copies of their immigration paperwork
recognising an authority in an unfamiliar jurisdiction
never_alone: a passport, visa or identity document — §4.9 already treats these as protected records in their own right and they belong to the identity safety domain, not to this one
a travel document or boarding pass
the word 'visa' — it also names a payment network
a foreign address or nationality

grouping_reasons: one application for one applicant — a purpose-coherent packet in exactly §3.9's sense, “content-incoherent but purpose-coherent”
a family's linked applications
an application with the decision and any challenge to it

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Applicant sits above application because one person may make several over years and their history is the useful unit. Note the tension with §3.8's rule against person-as-collector: this is a case where the person IS the subject rather than the author, which §3.8's own wording distinguishes.

collides_with.signal: the identity documents inside an immigration file are identity material in their own right. §4.9: “Rare but sensitive files such as passports, visas, and legal documents may be surfaced as protected records even when they do not meet a normal group-size threshold.”
collides_with.design_cite: §4.9 “Rare but sensitive files such as passports, visas, and legal documents may be surfaced as protected records”

collides_with.signal: an individual organising their own immigration paperwork is not running a casework file. Absence of a practice reference and a matter should route it to the personal side.

near-total overlap. 05 owns the applicant's own paperwork and already carries `applicant`, `route_or_category`, `application_reference` and `sponsor`. This entry claims only a practice's casework file. Slice 05 owns the party's own file; this slice owns the practitioner's. The mover is a practice-side signal — a matter reference, a fee-earner or counsel signature block, practice letterhead, an engagement letter. Absent one, this slice ABSTAINS and 05 wins. This is 05's own specialisation rule applied across the seam: 'the more specific domain wins where its own fields populate'.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Immigration files combine identity documents, family details and frequently accounts of persecution or hardship — §8.4's “identity documents” and “medical information” both routinely appear. No handling class is set here; see law.investigation's open_question.

entries.name: Family law matters
entries.one_line: Proceedings and agreements about relationships, children and the financial consequences of a family breaking down.

schema.example: the identifier of the proceeding
schema.why: Joins the file to its proceeding where one exists; much family work is done without any proceeding at all.

schema.example: the kind of family matter
schema.why: Read from the document's own heading. The available proceedings and their names differ profoundly by jurisdiction — some categories do not exist in some systems — so values are corpus-derived and none is equated here.

schema.example: an adult party to the matter
schema.why: Read from a caption or an agreement's parties block.

schema.example: a child the proceedings concern, where named
schema.why: Deliberately capped at `possible` and NEVER destination-eligible. A folder named after a child would put a minor's name into a directory listing, a search index and every UI surface. §3.8's rule against person-as-collector is reinforced here by §8.4's requirement that protected material 'should not display raw content in general group summaries'.

schema.example: the financial issues in the matter
schema.why: Prose. §3.6 requires the cited span before it becomes a fact.

deterministic: a captioned family-court document pairing a case identifier with a named family court or division
a financial disclosure form — labeled income, asset and liability fields — filed under a case identifier
an agreement whose operative provisions concern arrangements for children or division of family assets, carrying a matter reference
needs_llm: correspondence and statements with no caption, where the subject matter is the only signal
distinguishing a family agreement from an ordinary commercial one
recognising a family matter conducted entirely by email
never_alone: the words 'divorce', 'custody', 'separation' — they appear in journalism, fiction, counselling material and personal correspondence
a financial statement — §8.4's “account statements” belong to the finance domains unless a case identifier corroborates
names of family members
a marriage or birth certificate: those are identity documents (§4.9) before they are anything else

grouping_reasons: one family matter across its documents
the financial strand of a matter as a set
an agreement with the order that made it binding

template.why: §5.5's context rule, with 'issue strand' rather than any person-based level — see the `child_subject` field's reasoning. §5.9's scoped General branch is the right fallback for uncategorised material here rather than any label naming an individual.

collides_with.signal: family and estate planning documents overlap in a household's own records. The finance/admin slice owns a person's own will and family paperwork; this domain owns a practice's casework. Where a file is a household's own copy, this domain DEFERS.
a person's own divorce paperwork is their personal record. Absence of a practice reference and a matter should route it away from this slice.
a party's own family-court paperwork is 05's court-records or personal-slice material. This entry requires a practice-side signal.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase, and this is among the strongest cases for it in the whole catalogue: family files combine §8.4's “medical information”, “account statements” and “identity documents” with information about children. No handling class is set here; see law.investigation's open_question.

entries.name: Criminal defence files
entries.one_line: Acting for a person accused of an offence — the charge, the prosecution material, the defence case and the outcome.

schema.example: the identifier of the prosecution
schema.why: Joins the file to the proceeding. Criminal identifier formats differ from civil ones within the same jurisdiction, which is one more reason no pattern is authored here.

schema.example: the court the matter is before
schema.why: Criminal matters move between courts as they progress and the file must record which stage's court a document belongs to.

schema.example: the offence alleged, as stated on the charging document
schema.why: Read from the charging document's own text. This catalogue records what the document SAYS is alleged and asserts nothing about the accused.

schema.example: the person charged
schema.why: Capped at `possible` and never destination-eligible. A folder named after an accused person publishes an allegation in every directory listing; §8.4 requires that protected material “should not display raw content in general group summaries”, and a folder name is the most general summary there is.

schema.example: the stage the document belongs to
schema.why: Criminal procedure is stage-driven and the stage is normally stated. Stage names are jurisdiction-bound; values are corpus-derived.

deterministic: a charging or indictment document pairing a court, a case identifier and a stated offence
prosecution disclosure material delivered under a case identifier with a schedule of served and unused material
a custody, bail or sentencing document carrying a case identifier and a court name
needs_llm: defence working notes with no header
distinguishing prosecution material served on the defence from the defence's own work product
recognising a criminal matter from correspondence alone
never_alone: offence vocabulary — journalism, fiction, academic criminology and news alerts are full of it
a police reference number
the words 'charge', 'offence', 'arrest'
an identity document

grouping_reasons: one prosecution across its stages
prosecution material as one served set
the defence's own work product as a set

template.why: §5.5's context rule, with stage rather than any person-based level for the reason given under `accused`. Stage is genuinely how criminal files are worked, which makes the safer choice also the better one.

collides_with.signal: prosecution disclosure is a served document set with a schedule, structurally close to a production. The schedule vocabulary and the absence of a load file distinguish them.
an individual's own copies of their case paperwork are their personal records. Absence of a practice reference should route them away from this slice.
an accused person's own copies of court-issued documents are 05's. This entry requires a practice-side signal.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. A criminal file records an allegation against an identified person and frequently the personal details of complainants and witnesses. No handling class is set here; see law.investigation's open_question.

entries.name: Estates administration
entries.one_line: Administering a deceased person's estate — the grant, the assets and liabilities, and the distribution.

schema.example: the estate being administered
schema.why: The file's spine. Named on every document in the administration.

schema.example: the reference of the authority to administer
schema.why: The instrument that authorises everything else in the file. The instrument's name and format are jurisdiction-specific — some systems have no equivalent step at all — so no pattern is authored here.

schema.example: the person or institution administering
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule: the representative is often the client, sometimes the practice, and is never the deceased — three roles routinely conflated in these files.

schema.example: the stage of the administration
schema.why: Administration is a defined sequence and the stage is normally stated on the document. Values are corpus-derived because the sequence differs by system.

schema.example: the kind of asset a document concerns
schema.why: Estate files are organised around assets in practice. Read from the document's own subject line or heading.

deterministic: a grant or authority document naming an estate and a personal representative, issued by a named court or registry
an estate account — a statement of assets, liabilities and distributions headed with an estate name
correspondence with an asset holder citing an estate name and a grant reference
needs_llm: asset correspondence that names only the deceased and no estate reference
distinguishing estate administration from estate PLANNING done during a person's life, which shares vocabulary and parties
never_alone: a will — a person's own will is estate planning and belongs to the finance/admin slice; a will used in an administration acquires this domain only through the grant and the estate reference
a death certificate — an identity document first (§4.9)
the words 'estate' or 'beneficiary' — 'estate' also names real estate and 'beneficiary' appears in insurance and pensions
an account statement

grouping_reasons: one estate across its administration
asset correspondence by asset class
the accounts with the distributions they record

template.why: §5.5's context rule. Stage rather than asset class at the third level because an administration is worked as a sequence and stage is the dimension that stays meaningful when a file is reopened years later.

collides_with.signal: the lead brief assigns personal wills and estate planning to slice 05, and this domain DEFERS to it for everything done during the person's life. This domain begins at the administration and requires an estate reference or a grant to activate.
05 notes that a grant of representation is a court-issued document and an estate document at once. Agreed; this entry claims the practice's administration file built on that grant.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Estate files combine §8.4's “account statements” and “identity documents” with a deceased person's affairs and beneficiaries' personal details. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Property conveyancing
entries.one_line: Transferring or charging an interest in land — title, searches, contract, completion and registration.

schema.example: the land or premises
schema.why: The file's spine and the one thing every document in it shares. An address alone is weak; the title reference is what makes it precise.

schema.example: the registry's identifier for the title
schema.why: Land registration systems and their identifier formats are jurisdiction-specific, and some systems are deeds-based with no title number at all. The field is neutral; no pattern is authored here.

schema.example: which side the practice acts for
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule, and the field that decides how every document in the file is read: a search result means opposite things to a buyer and a seller.

schema.example: the stage the document belongs to
schema.why: Conveyancing is a strictly sequenced process and stage is how practitioners navigate the file. Stage names are jurisdiction-bound; values are corpus-derived.

schema.example: the date the transfer completed
schema.why: Stated on the completion statement and the transfer as a labeled slot. §3.10's narrow parsing applies.

deterministic: a title extract or register copy issued by a named land registry, carrying a title reference
a search result from a named authority citing a property address, filed alongside a matter reference
a transfer or conveyance instrument pairing a property description with parties and an execution block
needs_llm: an enquiry reply written as free correspondence
distinguishing a conveyancing file from a landlord's own tenancy paperwork or a homeowner's purchase folder
reading which side the practice acts for when only the correspondence shows it
never_alone: a property address — the corpus is full of addresses
a lease or tenancy agreement: a party's own lease belongs to the finance/admin slice
a floor plan or survey
the word 'property' — it also names an attribute in code and a characteristic in prose

grouping_reasons: one property transaction across its stages
searches as one bounded set
a chain of linked transactions

template.why: §5.5's context rule with the property as the spine, because one client may transact several properties and one property may be transacted repeatedly. §5.5's rule against time-first applies: completion dates would scatter a chain.

collides_with.signal: an owner's or tenant's own property paperwork — the signed lease, the mortgage statement — is that person's record and DEFERS to slice 05. This domain requires practice-side apparatus: searches, enquiries, a report on title, a matter reference.
a property transaction inside a larger corporate deal is a workstream of that deal. Where a code-named transaction exists, the deal domain is the better spine.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Conveyancing files combine addresses, identity documents and funding details — §8.4's “account statements” and “identity documents” both appear. No handling class is set here.

entries.name: Admission, licensing and continuing legal education
entries.one_line: A practitioner's own right to practise — admission, licensing, insurance and the education required to keep it.

schema.example: the body that admits or licenses
schema.why: The spine; a practitioner admitted in several places holds parallel obligations to each. Bodies and their names are jurisdiction-specific and are not enumerated here.

schema.example: the number the authority assigns
schema.why: Formats are per-authority. Corroboration required as elsewhere in this slice.

schema.example: admission | practising certificate | licence | insurance
schema.why: These have different renewal cycles and different consequences on lapse, and are routinely kept in one folder.

schema.example: the reporting period a record counts toward
schema.why: Continuing-education obligations are period-based and a record filed to the wrong period is effectively lost. Read from the certificate or the return.

schema.example: the course, session or activity attended
schema.why: Named on the completion certificate in a labeled slot, so `direct` per §3.5.

deterministic: a completion certificate naming a named accrediting body AND an activity AND a credit or hours value, addressed to a named practitioner
a practising certificate or licence document issued by a named authority carrying a practitioner identifier and a validity period
a compliance return pairing activities with a reporting period, addressed to an authority
needs_llm: course materials kept from an activity, with no certificate
distinguishing professional continuing education from ordinary employer training or academic study
never_alone: a completion certificate — every online course issues one and almost none are accredited legal education
the words 'CLE', 'CPD' or their equivalents alone: the abbreviations are used by many professions
a course name
a professional body's name in body text

grouping_reasons: one compliance period's activities and its return
all credentials from one authority
a credential with its renewals as a sequence

template.why: §5.5's context rule. This is the one entry in the slice where a period level is clearly right — the obligation IS periodic — but it still sits third, under the authority and the credential, because §5.5 keeps time below function for record domains.

collides_with.signal: slice 02 already has `career.professional-license` AND `career.certification` AND `career.continuing-education` — three entries covering exactly this material from the practitioner's own side. This entry survives only if the admitting-authority spine and the compliance-period structure are worth a legal-specific domain; otherwise it collapses into 02. See the open_question.

CLE materials look like course materials. §3.5's course rule fires on academic context; accredited professional education has an accrediting body and a compliance period instead, which is the distinguishing signal.
collides_with.design_cite: §3.5 “becomes a course fact only when the engine finds a course-code pattern together with academic context”

collides_with.signal: the direct duplicate. 02's entry owns continuing professional education for any profession; this entry would own only the legally-regulated form of it, keyed on an admitting authority. Weakest entry in this slice on that basis.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Licensing and disciplinary records are personal professional records about an identified individual. Most CLE certificates are not sensitive at all, which is again why the actual handling decision is P7's (§8.4) and not this catalogue's.
entries.open_question: This entry is the practitioner's OWN record, not a client's, and slice 02 already publishes `career.professional-license`, `career.certification` and `career.continuing-education` covering the same material. Should it exist here at all? It is retained because the admitting-authority spine and the compliance-period structure are specific to regulated legal practice and 02's entries are profession-neutral, but this is the entry a reviewer is most entitled to delete. Joseph's call: keep as a legal-specific specialisation, or drop and let slice 02 own it.

entries.name: Pro bono and publicly funded work
entries.one_line: Work done free or under public funding — the eligibility, the funding authority and the reporting that comes with it.

schema.example: pro bono | publicly funded | clinic | referred
schema.why: The only field that genuinely distinguishes this domain from law.matter-file, which is why this entry's open_question asks whether it is a domain at all.

schema.example: the body funding or certifying the work
schema.why: Publicly funded work is administered by jurisdiction-specific bodies with their own references and reporting; pro bono work often has a clearing organisation instead.

schema.example: the certificate or authorisation reference
schema.why: Authorises the work and bounds it. Formats are authority-specific; corroboration required.

schema.example: the clinic, charity or scheme the matter came from
schema.why: §3.8's roles rule: the referrer is not the client and is frequently the only organisation named on the file.
Pro bono matters are opened as matters and carry the same spine as everything else in this slice.

deterministic: a funding certificate or authorisation from a named funding body carrying a reference and a scope limit
an eligibility assessment form whose labeled fields pair means or merits criteria with an outcome
a scheme or clinic referral form naming a referring organisation and a client
needs_llm: a matter run pro bono with nothing on the file saying so
distinguishing a reduced-fee arrangement from genuinely unbilled work
never_alone: the phrase 'pro bono' — it appears in marketing material, firm brochures, CVs and award submissions far more often than in casework
absence of a bill
a charity's name
an eligibility form

grouping_reasons: one funded matter with its authorisation and reporting
all matters from one referral scheme
a reporting period's returns

template.why: §5.5's context rule. The dimension order is deliberately unusual — funding basis first — because that is the only arrangement under which this domain is distinguishable in a tree from law.matter-file, and seeing it written out is what makes the open_question below concrete.

collides_with.signal: this is a matter file with a funding overlay. Every other field is inherited. See the open_question.
publicly funded work has its own costs claims and reporting, which are billing artefacts under a different regime.

entries.sensitivity_why: §2.9's phrase. Eligibility assessments record a person's means and circumstances in detail — §8.4's “account statements” and “medical information” both routinely appear in them. No handling class is set here.
entries.open_question: Is pro bono a DOMAIN or a FACET on law.matter-file? Its schema is law.matter-file's plus a funding basis, a funding authority and a referral source, which is the profile of a facet rather than a domain. It is written as a domain here because the funding paperwork is a genuinely distinct document set with its own authority and its own reporting, but a reviewer could reasonably collapse it. If it collapses, `funding_basis` becomes a field on law.matter-file and the funding documents become work types there. Joseph's call.
